utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Sir Ivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic is handling the Defence this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, yes. We have your document which is hot off the press. What would you like to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to thank the Court for allowing us additional time this morning in order to make some changes and to try to have the affidavits comport with the Rules. On behalf of Dragan Kolundzija, we would formally like to advise the Tribunal Court we are not calling any live witnesses, and we would respectfully move the Court to accept the filing prepared today, October 8, 2001, and withdraw the filings made previously on October 3 and October 4, 2001. Briefing, the filing of today, October 8, 2001, include affidavits of 17 different individuals. They include three letters of prospective employment. They include two certificates reflecting that Dragan Kolundzija did not have any prior criminal record. And they also include two reports from doctors who have treated, evaluated, and diagnosed Dragan Kolundzija while here in the Detention Unit. This request is made in lieu of presentation of live evidence after consultation with my learned friend from the Office of the Prosecutor, Dirk Ryneveld, and in the interest of preserving judicial economy and efficiency as well as the resources available to the Tribunal, the affidavits are strictly used as further support of Mr. Kolundzija's conduct, demeanour, and reputation prior to, during, and after the tragic events the summer of 1992. Admittedly, some of the affidavits went beyond the issue of mitigation for which they are presented. The intent, purpose, and spirit of these affidavits is to address, explain, and clarify Mr. Kolundzija's reputation and character. It is hoped, and we respectfully request, since there is no objection, or presumably no objection, to the affidavits, letters of prospective employment, certificates reflecting no prior criminal record, and the two psychiatric reports, that they be accepted in lieu of live testimony and be given the same weight as evidence that was both live and through sworn transcripts. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ostojic. Before I call on the Prosecution. May I just ascertain whether any of the counsel for the other defendants have anything to say on this. Mr. Greaves?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: No. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ryneveld?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. At the outset, I can certainly agree with my learned friend that the Prosecution takes no objection to the concept of filing affidavits without the necessity of calling witnesses live for the various reasons that my friend has enunciated. The purpose of these affidavits, our understanding was, in order to provide character evidence, and we also understand that my friend has filed documents to show there's no previous criminal record and some reports. We take no issue with any of those matters, and as a matter of fact, we agree that provided that this provides the Court with the type of information it needs to make a fully informed sentencing decision, this is a preferable way, from the Prosecution's point of view, to save court time and so we can get on with further matters. I do have, however, some concern about the process that took place as I understand it, which was cause for some of the delay this morning, and that was that some time ago, my learned friends had filed affidavits. I had originally indicated to my learned friend that the affidavits were to be for the assistance of the Court on the issue of character and that I was not happy if they went beyond that, except if some of those witnesses would need to give some background information as to how it was that they knew Mr. Kolundzija in order to give some basis to the Court on facts in order to be able to express an opinion as respect to character. I understand that my friend had filed a series of affidavits, and I understand that those affidavits have now been the subject of an application for withdrawal and filing of additional documents or different documents. My friend has phoned me moments before court reopened this morning and told me what those changes were. Without getting into the details of those changes, the fact is that I have some concern that sworn affidavits have now been edited or changed and were not part -- exactly the same as the affiant swore to, apparently, when they were given. I have some concern about the process, and frankly, many of the changes that were made may well have been the topic of comment by the Prosecution in relation to submissions that might be made. So my position, on behalf of the Prosecution, is this: that those affidavits should be used for the purpose of character only, and where they go beyond the scope of character evidence, we would ask that the Court disregard those. And the facts upon which the guilty plea has been based has been recorded. It has been the subject of submissions by all counsel in writing. And where those character affidavits purport to go into factors beyond the issue of character, we would ask the Court to exercise its discretion, to disabuse your minds of those matters and treat it for the purpose for which it was filed. I believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: These affidavits come in under Rule 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ryneveld. Mr. Ostojic, I just wanted to ask you about the point made by Mr. Ryneveld. I think somebody has -- turn yours off. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is there a problem? Okay. Yes. I wanted to ask you about the point made by Mr. Ryneveld that some changes were made to the affidavits this morning, not necessarily with the authorisation of the affiants. Are these substantial changes, or are they editorial changes?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I can address that, Your Honour. First of all, as I told my learned friend Mr. Ryneveld, I did this weekend check with the affiants. There are six in particular that we believe minor editorial changes were made to those affidavits, and all told, I think, of those six affidavits, there were approximately no more than ten lines out of the complete set of six affidavits that were redacted from the original filing of October 3rd and 4th. In addition to a seventh affidavit, since he was a previous witness, we redacted his name as well from the original text to continue to protect his identity, as he had requested. So that would have been the seventh change. In all total, of the 24 affidavits, again only six changes were made. I can't comment on behalf of the OTP as to how they view some of these changes, but in my opinion, they were minor changes. I think they have no effect with respect to the issue for which they're presented, namely, the character and reputation of our client, Dragan Kolundzija, and I believe they continue to be consistent. With respect to those six, this weekend we did check with our investigator and made them verify with the affiants the changes that they were contemplating making, and as I told my learned friend this morning, that if necessary, we can get the affidavits from those individuals in order to make that attestation before the Court that they are in agreement with the redaction of those particular sentences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you give us again an outline of the context of this document? You don't have at the beginning of the document the contents. Just give us -- enumerate --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I will. The total number of affidavits are 24.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The total number of letters of employment or prospective employment are three; the number of certificates from the court and/or clerk of the jurisdiction where Mr. Dragan Kolundzija is from revealing no prior criminal record are two; and we have two psychiatric reports, which should correspond to the number of 31, which is the outline I believe that the Court has that we filed today, 31 separate documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I thank the clerk for that instruction and technology. In the original filing, you had, in my view, very usefully cited some passages from the transcripts. You have retained those?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Respectfully, Your Honour, I don't believe -- that was, I think, in the written brief that we've submitted but not in the original filing, which is clearly of just the affidavits and those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. Yes. Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We did not make any reference to the affidavits in the written brief. In particular, what we did was just generalise it for the Court in our sentencing brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have to consider the document that you have submitted, the affidavits and the other documents. We'll take those under consideration. But my understanding is that this constitutes your presentation today.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Mr. Ryneveld, do you have any submissions to make?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: If Your Honour is asking whether we're in a position to make our closing arguments at this point -- is that the question? We are in a position to do that whenever the Court wishes us to do that. I'm ready to do that now, should you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ryneveld. But you did use the term "closing arguments." We'd like to hear your submissions on this -- on the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: On the sentence, yes. Thank you. Well, with the Court's permission, perhaps I could just outline how the Prosecution intends to proceed with -- I was asking the Court's permission. I propose to commence by speaking about matters that are in common with respect to all three accused; that is, the camp conditions. I will then ask my co-counsel, Mr. Mundis, to deal with the issue of Sikirica, followed by Ms. Baly for Mr. Dosen, and then I will conclude with Kolundzija and any concluding remarks. I don't anticipate that collectively we will be more than half an hour, if that is acceptable to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honours are aware that the conditions in the camp were common to the guilty pleas of all three of these accused, and if I may, I just want to highlight some of the factors that are contained in the plea agreements and also with respect to the evidence that the Court has heard concerning the camp conditions. This Court is in a unique position on a sentencing, having heard substantially the evidence from the Prosecution witnesses on the issue and quite clearly that although counsel have made a recommendation to the Court, we are not attempting to usurp the function of the Court in any way, and the issue of pronouncing the just and appropriate and fitting sentence will always remain in the Court's hands and is not subject to recommendations of counsel. As Your Honours heard from the various witnesses, that once they arrived at Keraterm camp they were locked into one of three rooms. We've generally heard of Rooms 1, 2, and 3. And you've also heard that these rooms were terribly overcrowded. It was often the case that the detainees could not lie down and could not move about freely. And in particular, you heard about the men from the Brdo area, a number of days before the 25th of July, 1992, who had been segregated and placed in Room 3, and they were forced to endure particularly inhumane living conditions. With respect to the crowded conditions, you will recall the evidence of various witnesses that even when there was sufficient space to lie down in the rooms, the detainees did not have any suitable bedding. For example, one of the witnesses said the detainees slept on the concrete floor, and they sometimes had wooden pallets available to them and had to use grass as pillows. Now, additionally, you heard evidence that they were so overcrowded, not only with respect to area to sleep, but also that the air was stifling hot, and they couldn't get fresh air for many of the rooms. That was alleviated, of course, by the fact that the doors had bars on them, and then the ones closer to the barred doors would have access to the air. Now, they were allowed only to move when specifically permitted to do so and then usually only to receive what can best be termed as starvation rations. Often they were not provided opportunity to exercise and there was no regular routine whereby they would be permitted to regularly go outside of the rooms for fresh air. Just about every witness testified about the deplorable conditions at Keraterm camp. We know that Keraterm camp had few toilets and the toilets were in a terrible state of hygiene. There were no facilities for person hygiene. Food, when it was provided, was provided erratically, and when it was provided, it was inadequate. The water supply for the detainees was inadequate, particularly during the hot summer months, and they had no changes of clothing, no bedding, and with very rare exceptions, no medical care. You heard evidence that the detainees had at times to urinate or defecate in either a barrel that would be placed in the room or plastic bags in the room, since there was no access to toilets at night on many of the shifts. There were no facilities for bathing or washing clothes, and the majority of the detainees had lice. We did hear of some treatment that was offered on one occasion when a doctor came and provided some medication to combat the lice. The food rations, well, the daily rations we heard about were two thin slices of bread. Many of the witness testified that they were usually covered with flies since it had been left near the toilets before being fed to the detainees. The detainees were also provided with a bowl of water which occasionally, according to some, had a piece of cabbage or macaroni floating in it. Just about all of the detainees told you about the emaciated condition that they left the camp in. Many of them lost between 15 to -- I believe one witness indicated 30 kilos during the period of time that they were detained at Keraterm camp. Obviously, the quantity of food was totally inadequate. They were, when fed, were permitted only a minute or two to eat, and the quality of the food was very, very poor, and often there was not enough for everyone. Adding to that, that the other conditions in the camp, including the beatings on the various shifts, resulted in an atmosphere of terror, and that was part of the camp conditions. They were inhumane living conditions. Those, I believe, can be viewed as the common denominators for each of the three shifts. And accordingly, if I may at this point, I'm going to ask Mr. Mundis to address his attention to the accused Dusko Sikirica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, Dusko Sikirica, pursuant to the plea agreement in this case, has admitted that his role was commander of security at the Keraterm camp. And pursuant to that plea agreement and in his sentencing brief, Mr. Sikirica, through counsel, of course, has admitted that he had some, albeit limited, command responsibility attaching to him pursuant to his role as commander of security at the Keraterm facility. The Prosecution submits that viewed in light of both the evidence you've heard and in light of Mr. Sikirica's admissions as reflected in the plea agreement, that he was part of the command structure of the Keraterm camp. And there is also evidence, again reflected in the plea agreement, that on at least one occasion, Mr. Sikirica reported the misconduct of Zoran Zigic up the chain of command. The Prosecution submits that Mr. Sikirica certainly bears responsibility as commander of security for allowing outsiders to come into the camp, where the detainees were mistreated, beaten, killed, and otherwise abused. Certainly the evidence and what Mr. Sikirica has admitted to demonstrates that he was aware that outsiders were coming into the camp, and again on at least one occasion, he reported such misconduct to his senior authorities outside of the Keraterm camp. And certainly the Prosecution asserts that based on all of the evidence before you and the plea agreement, that Mr. Sikirica certainly had command responsibility or limited responsibility, even if it was limited, for the overall conditions in the camp, including the mistreatment that occurred of detainees. But certainly Mr. Sikirica's role is not limited to his role as the commander of security at the Keraterm camp. Mr. Sikirica has personally admitted that he killed one of the detainees by shooting him. And although the Defence in their sentencing brief has remarked that the victim most likely was killed instantaneously and that the victim hadn't suffered any humiliation or had been tormented prior to being shot by the accused Sikirica, the Prosecution certainly asserts, on the other hand, that nor was this -- had this detainee -- is there any evidence that this detainee provoked this killing in any way. What we have here is simply an incident where the accused Sikirica murdered this individual without any justification whatsoever. He did this in broad daylight. He did this while other detainees were present and were aware of this. And the Prosecution submits that this certainly contributed to the overall atmosphere of terror which existed in the Keraterm camp during the summer of 1992. In addition to this single killing, however, the accused has acknowledged that there were countless other killings that occurred in the camp, to include the Room 3 massacre, which I'll talk about in a few moments. Clearly this was a camp where, again, countless numbers of individuals were murdered and where, in the Prosecution's view, the accused, as the commander of security, and able, however limited his role was, to allow insiders or outsiders to gain access to this camp, certainly in our view is an aggravating factor. Beyond these killings, however, there were also countless individuals who were beaten and tormented and abused inside the Keraterm camp. We have had the accused Sikirica admit that women were sexually raped, were raped and other sexual assaults occurred inside the Keraterm camp. And as Mr. Ryneveld has aptly described for you, the conditions in the camp were certainly intolerable for those men and few women who were actually detained there. With respect to the Room 3 massacre, you heard evidence in this trial that that event was committed by outsiders, and again, based on his role as commander of security, the Prosecution asserts that the accused Sikirica, who has admitted that he had a technical duty to prevent outsiders from entering the camp, should be held at least partially responsible for that massacre on the grounds that he did have, as commander of security, the ability to control who came into the Keraterm camp. Your Honour, the Prosecution asserts that the accused Sikirica could have done more to both improve the conditions in the camp and to control access to the camp by the outsiders that the evidence has shown came into the camp and committed crimes against the people that were detained there, and he failed in that duty to do everything that he could to alleviate the suffering that went on in the camp. Your Honour, for the next part of my brief submissions, I would ask that we go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, in light of the submissions of the Prosecution, both orally this morning and pursuant to our written sentencing brief that was filed on the 28th of September, as well as pursuant to the plea agreement, the Prosecution respectfully requests that the accused Sikirica be sentenced to a term of imprisonment of 17 years. If there are no further questions with respect to Mr. Sikirica, I would respectfully ask that my co-counsel, Ms. Baly, continue with respect to the accused Damir Dosen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mundis. Ms. Baly.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Your Honours, what I intend to do is not to address matters that I've already addressed in the Prosecution's written submissions but to focus on a number of issues raised by counsel for the accused Damir Dosen in their written submissions and respond to those issues. Firstly, Your Honours will recall from our written submissions that the Prosecution's position insofar as Damir Dosen's position in the camp is that Damir Dosen did occupy a position of trust. The counsel for the accused Damir Dosen take issue with that particular submission and argue against that, saying that he did not occupy such a position. Whilst the Prosecution do agree, in accordance with the plea agreement, that the accused held no superior rank in a formal or de jure sense, there is also agreement in the plea agreement between the parties that the accused did act as a shift leader and that he did have authority over between 6 to 12 guards. This does, in the Prosecution's submission, constitute a position of superiority in a de facto sense, namely, that despite his lack of rank, he acted as a superior or a leader within the camp. In addition, the Prosecution submits that it is entirely appropriate for this Court to consider the fact that this accused was in fact a reserve police officer at the relevant time, and it is submitted this position does carry with it responsibilities toward all citizens. And Your Honours will recall the evidence given by the expert called by the Defence that on this point the office of police officer [sic] obliged the person holding such an office to prevent mistreatment to all citizens. It is submitted that it would be artificial for Your Honours not to consider the fact that the accused was indeed a police officer when he occupied his position and when he committed the crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Your submission is that he had de facto Article 7(3) responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: It's in accordance with 7(1). The submission is that he did occupy a position of trust vis-a-vis the detainees within the camp and that that factor is a factor for Your Honours to take into account in aggravation, as an aggravating factor, the fact that he occupied this position of trust as a superior and that he breached the trust reposed in him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Not under 7(3).

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Under 7(1).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Under 7(1).

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Under 7(1). If I can turn now, Your Honours, to some matters raised insofar as mitigation is concerned. And the first matter concerns the submission that the accused makes that he should be given -- that considerable weight should be given to remorse expressed by the accused. There is indeed evidence that this accused did express some remorse to the detainees whilst he was in Keraterm. There is also evidence - and it's referred specifically to in the written submissions - that this accused said that what happened to the prisoners, the detainees in Room 3, was something that they had deserved. And so any remorse expressed at the time the offences were committed should be balanced, in the Prosecution's submission, against that evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What was the time frame within which that statement was made --

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: That statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- in relation to other expressions of remorse?

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: That statement was made after, Your Honour, after the Room 3 massacre had taken place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have to consider, though, the whole position about remorse. And usually the fact that somebody pleads guilty is some indication, at least, of remorse.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Yes. And, Your Honour, I'm about to turn to that, if I may. The point raised by the accused at paragraph 36 of the written submissions is indeed a good one, a very good one, and the Prosecution agrees with it. It is important that this accused has acknowledged his guilt. It is important -- it is an important acknowledgment that a person of Serbian ethnicity from the Prijedor region has admitted that he committed this crime. It is indeed a very rare acknowledgment. It is important to the victims of Keraterm camp, for the region of Prijedor in general, and hopefully, Your Honours, for the process of reconciliation. There is some difficulty in that this expression is not supported by anything further. Indeed, if Your Honours consider the psychiatric report dated the 2nd of October, there is an absence of any expression of remorse. In fact, quite -- the report suggests quite the contrary. The expression of remorse is somewhat empty, in the Prosecution's submission, and loses some of its force because it's not supported in any way from anything from the accused's mouth. The accused in this case has asked Your Honours to find that at the time of the offence, he was of a diminished capacity. And whilst they do not ask Your Honours to take that into account in terms of any finding of not guilty, they have asked Your Honours to take it into account in mitigation and to impose upon the accused a lighter sentence. In the Prosecution's submission, the accused has failed to establish that he was, in fact, of diminished mental capacity at the time the offences took place. Albeit the accused only need establish it on the balance of probabilities, the evidence of the expert -- of the three experts to which Your Honours may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please continue, Ms. Baly.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: The evidence from the three experts too that were given during the trial and one recently by way of report does not refer to the term "diminished mental capacity" in any sense, in any respect, and the most, in the Prosecution's submission, Your Honours could find is that the accused is now suffering from post-traumatic stress disorder. The evidence that the accused suffered various stress reactions which have indeed led, it seems, to this condition of post-traumatic stress disorder. It's noteworthy that the various stress reactions did not occur whilst the accused was in Keraterm camp. And, in fact, the accused was able to continue his duties even after the Room 3 massacre up until after the camp was closed. In addition, after he left Keraterm camp, he was able to function as a member of society in a condition which allowed him to participate in the army on the front line and later to be employed as a guard in a discotheque. It is further submitted - and this is an inference that I would ask Your Honours to draw from the evidence - that much of the stress that the accused has suffered he has suffered as a result of the circumstances that he now finds himself in. They manifested after he became aware that he was under investigation and after he was taken into custody. At most the evidence established that he is suffering from post-traumatic stress disorder, not diminished mental capacity, and for those reasons, Your Honours should not mitigate the sentence in light of any mental incapacity. Similarly, the accused asks Your Honours to consider his personal hardship that he suffered whilst in Keraterm and since Keraterm in mitigation, sentence. It is conceded by the Prosecution that he did in fact suffer considerable personal hardship; however, there is a failure on the part of the accused to link such hardship to the offences, the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. offences that occurred in Keraterm, and it is, therefore -- whilst it is a subjective factor that Your Honours can take into account, it does not, in the Prosecution's submission, justify a significant reduction in sentence. Your Honours, at this point may I ask that the Court move into closed session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: In summation, Your Honours, the Prosecution does maintain that the crime committed by this accused was committed whilst he was in a position of trust, and it is, therefore, an aggravated crime. The participation of the accused in the repressive system that operated in Keraterm camp - and Mr. Mundis and Mr. Ryneveld have outlined essentially the nature of that system - justifies, in the Prosecution's submission, a sentence of seven years imprisonment. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Baly. Mr. Ryneveld, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. As I indicated earlier, I propose to deal with the accused Kolundzija and then a very brief concluding remarks. It's trite law to say that each case turns on its own unique and individual facts, but especially with respect to the accused Kolundzija, that is very much the case. Mr. Kolundzija has pled guilty, and with respect to his role in the persecution of the detainees during their confinement at Keraterm between the 24th of May and the 5th of August, 1992, and the Court has accepted that guilty plea. Now, the Court again has had the benefit of hearing all of the evidence from the various witnesses, and the Court has also had the benefit of reading the plea agreement between the parties and the facts which the parties agree apply as against the accused Kolundzija. I've already outlined for you the camp conditions that prevailed during that time period, and Mr. Kolundzija started out as a guard during part of that time period and then accepted a promotion to shift leader, fully aware and fully cognisant of the fact that the conditions at Keraterm were inhumane. I don't think that it's stating -- overstating the matter to say that the conditions at Keraterm camp were in fact a living hell for the detainees who were there. Many of the detainees died as a result of beatings and -- that they sustained at the hands of not only guards but visitors to the camp. Now, against the background that I have outlined to the Court of the inhumane conditions, we need to examine Mr. Kolundzija's particular role, and we would submit that the bulk of the evidence would indicate that Mr. Kolundzija did not personally mistreat any of the detainees, nor was there evidence that the guards on his shift, to his knowledge, mistreated the detainees. We have had many detainees come forward during the course of the evidence, even for the Prosecution, and indicated that -- of the good things that Mr. Kolundzija did for them while on his shift. Those are all mitigating circumstances. Those are all matters that not only I'm sure the Court will take into consideration but that the Prosecution has taken into consideration in making its submissions and making its recommendation to the Court. There is some evidence, however, that Mr. Kolundzija gave preferential treatment to some of the prisoners, some of the people that he knew, people he knew around Prijedor, neighbours, friends who -- you recall hearing the evidence how he allowed some people to use the telephone to call their families. He permitted -- generally permitted families of the prisoners to bring food to supplement their obvious inadequate diet at Keraterm. We have heard many factors in evidence from the Prosecution witnesses, many of whom were the detainees on his shift, who came forward to say good things about Mr. Kolundzija. Some of them went so far as to say that Kole, which was his nickname, Kole's shift was the best shift. But it must be remembered, however, that even though his shift may have been the best shift, nevertheless, the conditions were terrible and inhumane. And not only did Mr. Kolundzija know of the bad conditions, but he didn't quit in protest. No. He in fact accepted a promotion from guard to shift leader.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld, can I stop you?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It wasn't clear to me what is the significance of the point you're making about the preferential treatment that he gave to people that he knew. Are you advancing that as something that the Chamber should take into consideration, and if so, in what way?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. The Prosecution position is that Mr. Kolundzija was not universally giving privileges to all of the detainees. We know, for example, that the men from the Brdo area were kept in their rooms for days on end and the logistics of it would show that during Mr. Kolundzija's shift, those prisoners were also detained and would have been kept without exercise, would have been kept without food and water and be detained in their premises. The people that came forward to say that he did things on their behalf were almost invariably - and I agree that there were some exceptions - but almost invariably people he knew, friends that he knew, neighbours he knew, and that he gave privileges to some but not to everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Wouldn't it be correct to say that his acts of kindness were confined to people whom he knew?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I do not think that I would be characterising it completely correctly if I were to say that his acts of kindness were confined to those, because there were some -- there was some evidence from some of the witness that indicated that he allowed others also to use the phone, he allowed other families also to bring food, and I could not say conclusively that that was only for people that he knew. But quite clearly, people that he knew got preferential treatment. It may be that some others also received privileges, but we cannot say conclusively that he only allowed his friends or neighbours or family to receive those privileges. But the submission is that if you knew Kole, you were in a much better position to receive favourable treatment. Now, as I was about to go into that -- he accepted the position from guard to shift leader in full knowledge that these beatings and murders were taking place and were likely to continue and in full knowledge that the camp conditions were horrendous. He could see the condition of the detainees. I mean, their emaciation was a progressive case. They were unkempt. He could see the results of the injuries, the bodies in the morning, the fact that people needed treatment, the fact that people were bruised and beaten when he came on his shift. These matters could not and did not, we would submit, escape his attention, and yet he stayed. He stayed. He made a personal choice to stay on as opposed to quit in protest and do what he ought to have done and not have been part of the system that was in place that was for persecution. Now, by way of mitigating circumstances, apart from the things I've already outline, the facts that he made -- he obviously gave many acts of kindness. He admitted his guilt by entering a guilty plea, and he did so -- although he did so after the case had been fully presented for the Prosecution. He has saved the Trial Chamber some valuable time by pleading guilty and by proceeding as he has done this afternoon or this morning by filing affidavits and not calling a Defence case. It would have been preferable had he done so earlier in the proceedings; however, the Prosecution would acknowledge that some credit should be given to him for the timing of the entry of the plea before presenting his full Defence case. Now, my co-counsel Ms. Baly has made reference to the fact that Mr. Dosen, in his role as police officer, as a reserve police officer, had an obligation to protect people, and we would submit that Mr. Kolundzija was in exactly same situation. One would expect that police officers have a duty to protect, and instead, we know the conditions under which these detainees were kept. Now, persecution is a very serious crime, and it is deserving of a sentence that reflects the abhorrence of the crime, that imposes a just penalty and acts as a deterrence for others of like mind, in our respectful submission. And as I've outlined earlier, that each case must turn on its own unique and individual facts. And given the evidence and given the plea agreement and given Mr. Kolundzija's lack of personal involvement in beatings, we would submit that an appropriate and just sentence in this case is five years' imprisonment. We would also submit, Your Honours, that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Ryneveld, that you are not in agreement, obviously, with the last submission of the Defence on this, which is that taking into consideration the entire set of circumstances, Mr. Kolundzija be given a sentence which, taking account of the time he has already served, would result in his immediate release. That would be a sentence, then, of about two years and, I think, perhaps nine months.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I've indicated, it is for the Court to determine what is a just and fitting sentence; it's for counsel to make recommendations. Our position is that the crime of persecution is one that must be viewed as being extremely serious, and one must look at what is the lowest basic acceptable sentence for a crime of this nature. And in the Prosecution's view, of course, it's a recommendation to this Court that this type of sentence has to show to the International Community and the world at large that persecution is a significant, serious offence, and that although, admittedly, Mr. Kolundzija's conduct is at the low end of the scale of seriousness of persecution, nevertheless, in our submission, a just and fitting sentence would be a sentence of no less than five years. So in summary, then, Your Honour, as my co-counsel -- we would rely on our written submission that was filed on the 28th of September, and we, of course, have in our very brief submissions, oral submissions to you today, not dealt exhaustively with the factors contained in our Prosecution sentencing brief. But by way of concluding remarks, the Prosecution asks that you impose a sentence of 17 years for Mr. Sikirica, a sentence of 7 years for Mr. Dosen, and a sentence of 5 years for Mr. Kolundzija. Those are our submissions. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ryneveld. Mr. Greaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: May it please Your Honours. I'm going to address you, I hope and finish by 1.00. Immediately before I pose what I have to say to Your Honours, the accused Dusko Sikirica would seek Your Honours' permission to address you very briefly on his own behalf, if you would find that acceptable, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, that would be acceptable.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'm grateful. Your Honour, I first want to deal with the issue of the guilty plea tendered by the defendant and what credit should be given for that. In so doing, I am, of course, conscious of the case of Prosecutor versus Stevan Todorovic, in which each of Your Honours was involved in July of this year, and in particular paragraph 81 of that decision, which if I can briefly remind Your Honours, says this: "A guilty plea is always important for the purpose of establishing the truth in relation to a crime. Generally, however, a plea of guilt will only contribute to the above-described public advantage ..." And that is the public advantage, if I can give a shorthand phrase for it, of judicial economy and the saving of time and saving of witnesses giving evidence. "... the above-described public advantage if it is pleaded before the commencement of the trial against the accused. Needless to say, if pleaded at a later stage of the proceedings or even after the conclusion of the trial, a voluntarily admission of guilt will not save the International Tribunal the time and effort of a lengthy investigation and trial." Your Honours, it's in the context of that observation in that judgement that I now address you, and I seek to persuade you that in this case, it would be right to give the accused full or, at the very least, substantial credit for his having pleaded guilty in this case, albeit at the end and after the conclusion of the evidence against him. It is important, in our submission, to go back and look at what the position was at the outset of the trial. At that stage, the Prosecution was asserting against this accused not just the offences of persecution and other offences but also the offence of genocide, and it was being placed on a factual basis which we submit was far more serious than that in fact has come out during the course of the evidence and has been accepted on all sides in the plea agreement, and one only has to look at the way in which the Prosecution were putting their case at the outset, both in their pre-trial brief and their opening statement, to see how the matter was put against the accused. It is also important to remember that many elements that go to the issue of persecution also go equally to the issue of genocide. Not just did the case against Dusko Sikirica at that time involve Keraterm and the events that transpired in the summer of 1992 at that place, but also linked the defendant not just to a massacre in Trnopolje but to wider events: for example, ethnic cleansing in Kozarac; for example, the plan, if such existed, in relation to the takeover of power in Prijedor in 1992. To put not too fine a point on it, at that point it is quite evident, we submit, that there would have been no prospect whatsoever of any basis for agreement between the Prosecution and the Defence as to either plea or as to any factual basis for such a plea, and that is effectively affirmed by the Prosecution in the way in which they came to their agreement with the defendant in respect of plea. The parties were, in short, simply too far apart. In any event, there was never any prospect whatever that the defendant would plead guilty to genocide, and that matter would have had to have been tried in any event, hearing, we submit, the very same witnesses that have in fact given evidence. At that stage also, the jurisprudence, we would submit, was wholly against encouraging anybody to plead guilty. The case of Erdemovic is often cited by those who say, "Well, there has been jurisprudence from the word 'go' saying that you get credit for pleading guilty," but many advocates on this side of the bar would say that Erdemovic is in fact very much on its own facts, unique and dependent upon the very unusual circumstances in that case. And even if there was encouragement in Erdemovic from the learned judge, Judge Cassese, for people to plead guilty, such encouragement was effectively destroyed by the case of Jelisic, in which the defendant pleaded guilty but, as far as everybody could see, didn't exactly get a great deal of credit for having done that. And so at that time this trial started, there was no substantial jurisprudence with which any advocate could properly, within the confines of his professional duty, could properly go to a defendant and say, "This is what happens if you plead guilty." So what do we have and how should we approach this particular circumstance which, we respectfully submit, is, in the history of this Tribunal, thus far unique, a defendant pleading guilty after the close of evidence against him? What I would like to do is to draw an example from the system from which I and the learned judge, Judge May come, not because I'm necessarily advancing it as the national judicial system which is inevitably the best of the lot, but because the way in which the English system deals with this particular problem is one which might assist the Tribunal as a whole to develop its jurisprudence in relation to guilty pleas. When you come to sentence a defendant under the English system, there are three possibilities as to how the basis for sentence may be determined. The first is where a defendant pleads not guilty to the crimes alleged against him and there is a trial before a jury. It results in conviction, and the judge is then able to sentence the defendant according to the evidence heard at that trial. In those circumstances, the defence has very little scope for advocating any particular view of the facts. The judge has heard the evidence, can make his own mind up as to how serious the facts which have been heard are, and can sentence accordingly. The second circumstance is that the defendant pleads guilty and accepts, without reservation, all the material and significant facts alleged against him by the Prosecution, or comes to an agreement which is rendered into writing on those facts. Again, the judge is fully equipped to sentence accordingly at that point. There is no dispute about the facts. They are known. And the learned judge can come to his own conclusion. It's the third circumstance, which I want to deal with in some detail and which may assist Your Honours to see how this particular defendant can be viewed, the defendant pleads guilty but he does so on a factual basis which is not accepted by the Prosecution. Let me give an example and one which is not uncommon: An assault is alleged against the accused. He admits taking part in that assault but denies, as some witnesses allege, that he took part in the kicking of the victim. And kicking a victim in the English courts is regarded as a serious and aggravating feature of an assault. The Prosecution does not accept that the particular defendant was not involved in kicking, and therefore the trial judge orders that there should be a trial of an issue, the issue being: did the defendant kick the victim or not, or did he simply take part in another way? The matter is then heard by the judge sitting alone without a jury, and the judge hears evidence, prosecution evidence, and the defendant himself can give evidence and call evidence. At the conclusion of that hearing, the judge delivers a very short oral judgement indicating what facts he found to be true and the basis upon which he intends to sentence the defendant. At that point the Defence can then address the judge on sentence accordingly. If he finds substantially against the defendant on the facts, or completely against the defendant on the facts, it is likely that the defendant will lose some, if not all, of his credit for having pleaded guilty. How may we examine that situation and relate it to what has happened here? There has been, of course, a full contest of the indictment. As regards the most serious matters, the defendant has successfully defended the two counts which involve genocide. We submit that the defendant has been able, through the hearing of evidence, not only successfully to defend the issue of genocide but also to defend the extent of his involvement in these matters. And I refer back again to the way in which - and it's important to look at - the way in which the Prosecution were putting the case against him in respect of his role in the camp and his activities there and his activities outside the camp. There are a number of grave allegations which we respectfully submit now no longer need to trouble the Trial Chamber; for example, an allegation that he personally killed 18 to 20 people after the Room 3 massacre, another allegation of an allegation of rape by him personally. If one looks at paragraph 5 of the plea agreement, we respectfully submit that one can see that it has come about only because we have, in fact, heard the evidence, and it's quite apparent that the position that we have now reached could not have been reached at the outset and simply being done on the basis of written statements being provided or extracts of written statements being provided to the Trial Chamber. Let me give you an example: The Prosecution's case, as we understood it at the outset, was that the defendant had been the commander of the camp at Keraterm throughout the period of the indictment that was alleged against him. We respectfully submit that, as far as that is concerned, we have now been able to establish, and it is agreed, that the dates of his duty at Keraterm were in fact in accord with the alibi advanced by him. That we would not have been able to do but for the hearing of evidence. And I remind you briefly about the substantial evidence of the defendant being at the Prijedor hospital at the end of July and beginning of August 1992 and evidence, some of it from a Prosecution witness, putting him at a checkpoint at Hambarine prior to the 14th of June, 1992. We respectfully submit that the defendant has by the hearing of evidence been able to achieve a factual position, as well as a position on the indictment that would not have been available to him at the outset. So what the hearing of evidence has achieved here is that we've been able to arrive at a position on the facts that lies between the positions held respectively by the Defence and Prosecution at the outset of this case. In those terms, a proper reflection of what happened and what the defendant's role in what happened has only been achieved by being able to hear that evidence. The consequences of that are that the Trial Chamber is enabled, having heard the evidence to arrive, firstly, at a position which results from what is called often and one hears frequently, the truth-finding process. That's only been able to be achieved by the giving of evidence, and it's achieved what ultimately must be seen as a just position, because it's only justice if a man is sentenced on the basis of facts which are established and are accepted as being an accurate and proper reflection of those facts. For those reasons, we respectfully urge the Trial Chamber to say that taking all those circumstances into account, that he can properly be treated in the unusual and particular circumstances of this case, and it may be that you would want to say this should not necessarily be taken as a green light for everybody to have a trial and then put their hands up at the end of it, but in the particular circumstances of this case, we would invite you to say that he can properly be treated on this count of persecution as if he had pleaded guilty at the outset and had subsequently had a trial on issues of fact alone. As I say, it may well be that Your Honours would want to take an opportunity to develop somewhat the jurisprudence of the Tribunal to enable advocates who defend in this Tribunal to have a clear road map so that we can deal with situations where an accused admits significant facts which place him within the purview of a crime but where they significantly differ from a version being asserted by the Prosecution. It was for that reason that I told you of the English system. There may be aspects of that which can be improved upon, but I suggested it as perhaps - and I hope - a helpful framework on which to build some jurisprudence or even formal rules relating to guilty pleas. I rely also on the submissions we've made in writing to this particular aspect. I turn now to issues of fact in the case. There are, of course, a number of factual issues which have been raised in the sentencing brief of the Prosecution. The position that we invite Your Honours to take is set out in our sentencing brief. In essence, it is that where facts are asserted which are at variance with the plea agreement, it should be the plea agreement which prevails. We rely in particular on the course that Your Honours adopted in the Todorovic case, which was to refuse both parties to call witnesses who on the face of it were going to counter matters that are going to be set out and agreed in the plea agreement. I want now, as I indicated in the sentencing brief, just to deal with a number of matters of fact in relation to the Prosecution brief. Can I, first of all, deal with paragraph 27 of their brief, please. The assertion is made that -- and the impression left is that the business of rounding up prisoners, arresting people, and confining them in Keraterm was an exclusively and always was an exclusively Serb activity. Your Honours will recall that there was evidence in the case that one of the people who eventually ended up as a victim of murder was a non-Serb policeman, a Croat by the name of Drago Tokmadzic, who was at one stage involved himself in the rounding up of people and bringing them to Keraterm. So there was a time when some people who were not Serb were perfectly happy to be involved in the process that was taking place. Events consumed them as well; of that there is no doubt. But to portray this as an exclusively Serb activity is, we respectfully submit, somewhat misleading. Paragraph 28. The Prosecution refers to the headquarters of Keraterm camp. With the very greatest of respect to them, that is to give it a name that really over-dignifies it and really does not matter the physical reality of that particular building, a weigh hut. Your Honours have photographs of that produced by both the Prosecution and the Defence, and you can look at it. The fact that it was a weigh hut and the size it was goes, we submit, to indicate what the real importance of this security detachment was, the real importance of Dusko Sikirica and his men. They were made to go and sit in a little weigh hut at some distance from the main building. Meanwhile, the inspectors who were responsible for conducting interviews and interrogations with those detained, they occupied and had full run of the proper offices in the main building. The headquarters was, in reality -- the headquarters of this facility was, in reality, at Prijedor II police station, the place in which Zivko Knezevic had his office and from where he, we submit, administered Keraterm facility, Keraterm camp. The Prosecution rely on three witnesses in relation to describing it as the headquarters. I think, if I'm not mistaken, that we didn't actually hear the word "headquarters" used by witnesses to describe that particular weigh hut. I'm not going to read the particular transcript references that are relied upon by the Prosecution, but I urge Your Honours to look at it because you will see that they are remarkably innocuous in the way in which they describe that particular building. So to dignify it with the word "headquarters," we submit, is a serious case of over-egging the pudding. Also in paragraph 28, it is asserted that he was in a position of superior authority to everyone else present in the camp. With great respect, that is simply not in accordance with the evidence in this case. He cannot be superior to the inspectors who were present in the camp carrying out the interrogations since they were officers of superior rank in the same force as he. And Your Honour will recall hearing evidence from one of those gentleman as to the way in which they would come and go into the camp. He cannot be, we submit, superior to the military because the military are plainly not under his command and plainly he is not a military officer able to give orders to the military. Of course he has a duty to visitors, to keep out those who are not authorised and so on. But visitors are not under his command. His duty in relation to visitors extends only thus far: to keep them out if they are not authorised. Also in paragraph 8 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I imagine, Mr. Greaves, that what was meant was that he had a position of superiority in relation to those who were more or less permanently in the camp as distinct from those who came and went.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes. And plainly those who are part of the shifts fall into that category, although with the caveat that we have raised in our written brief about the actual nature, as opposed to the putative nature, of that authority. As far as the comment about clear lines of command and control are concerned, again we respectfully submit that that must be read very carefully in the light of the plea agreement in fact reached as to what the nature of his role was and the nature and extent of his authority. Paragraph 29, the Prosecution assert -- make an assertion about property being confiscated. I don't dispute that. Can I remind the Trial Chamber that in relation to one item in particular, we heard quite a lot of evidence that identity cards were taken from detainees and subsequently were returned to them. The observation is made that many of the detainees had any remaining personal property confiscated and then were beaten. It's right that two people whom the Prosecution single out mentioned the existence of beatings upon arrival. We would respectfully submit that it is remarkable in this case how little evidence, in fact, was given by all of the people who were detainees at Keraterm of being beaten upon arrival, and I am able, because I was involved in the Celebici case, to contrast those two cases where almost universally witnesses, Serb witnesses who were detained by the Muslims, were in fact beaten at a particular wall upon arrival. This case, we submit, is not insignificant for the fact that remarkably little evidence was in fact given of people being beaten upon arrival. Indeed we would submit that it was the exception, not the rule. Paragraph 31, the second sentence and third sentence uses the word "inspectors" in inverted commas, as if there was somehow not a proper description of those people. Again, you'll hear -- you've heard from many people who were interviewed, interrogated at Keraterm who described the people doing it as such, and indeed you heard from one individual who did that job. And we respectfully submit that it's a proper description of what their position was. It wasn't challenged during the course of the case as being -- by the Prosecution as being a proper description. The assertion is made that beatings regularly accompanied interrogation. We submit that that is not the evidence in the case, and it is not supported by the transcript of this matter. There were, of course, one or two witnesses who spoke of having been hit by a guard whether going to or from an interrogation, and one or possibly two, as I recall it, spoke of some physical ill-treatment during the course of interrogation. However - and Your Honours will recall there was some considerable evidence given by witnesses about interrogations - that was certainly not, we submit, the regular accompaniment to interrogation. Had it been so, the issue of torture might have been a quite different one in the event the Prosecution had to concede that torture was not one -- a case that was supported by the evidence. Why did they do that? They did so because there wasn't a pattern of beatings during interviews, interrogation, and so I'd invite Your Honours to ignore that particular point. Paragraph 32 asserts that after being beaten, detainees received no medical treatment. Again, with great respect to the Prosecution, that is not accurate. We have heard from a number of witnesses, and in particular the Prosecution tried to rely on the activities of Dusko Sikirica at the hospital as founding part of the case against him -- at the hospital when some detainees were in fact taken there for hospital treatment. No doubt Your Honours will recall that evidence. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Paragraph 33. Whilst one doesn't dispute that necessarily as a proposition, I would invite Your Honours to remember the evidence of Witness Z and the evidence of a number of detainees who spoke, for example, of bodies being collected in the hearse which was set aside for the particular purpose of collecting bodies and taking them before the war to the cemetery and of those detainees who had been killed who were spoken of by Witness Z as having been given if not perfect burials, at least dignified and decent burials in a regular cemetery. That, of course, is not to avoid the point that many people were killed, and we accept that, and many people who were killed did not receive such burials. But that particular aspect should be viewed in full, not on the selective basis that we say the Prosecution have advanced. Finally paragraph 34. The Prosecution use the phrase "The Serb authorities fired on the occupants of Room 3 with machine-guns." Again, the evidence on exactly where and what their position was, the position of the perpetrators of that particular massacre, is not, we submit, on the evidence clear, and it is not proved beyond reasonable doubt that it was the authorities. It may equally have been a freelance activity conducted for whatever reason - we don't know - by those who decided to come in and perpetrate it. We would respectfully submit that to use the phrase "the Serb authorities" is erroneous on the evidence in this case. I turn now briefly not to the Prosecution sentencing brief but to some remarks made about conditions. And again I shall be, hopefully, brief. Firstly, submissions in relation to the food. My learned friend Mr. Ryneveld asserted that you've heard the Prosecution evidence about that. It's unfortunate that he chose to avoid mentioning the fact that there was a certain amount of Defence evidence given about that, which no doubt assisted him and his colleagues to come to the conclusion that they did on the plea agreement concerning food. Finally this: Observations are made about his duty to prevent people from coming in. Of course that is the job of a commander of security. That is plainly right. But again, if one is sentencing this man on the basis of what he did or failed to do, one must ask this question: Are duty and ability the same thing or different things? He may have had the duty, but in our submission, his ability to prevent people from coming in was seriously restricted. If you take an individual like Zoran Zigic, who is on trial in another case, and you are faced with an individual of murderous bent like that, a man who plainly had a substantial enthusiasm for killing, on the evidence in this case, it takes a very brave man indeed to stand up to him and say, "You're not coming in here today." I wonder how many of us in this room would have felt able to do that, faced with a man of the disposition and character of Zoran Zigic. I suspect it might be remarkably few. Moving on now to some brief remarks about Dusko Sikirica. This is a matter that I've discussed with my learned friends. I don't think it is formally in evidence, but I think it the subject of no contest by them, that the defendant was a man of otherwise good character in the sense of never having been convicted of offences of any kind in the past. He is a family man, two children, both young, both of school age. And Your Honours will also wish to bear in mind in sentencing him the character evidence given the Defence case. And I don't intend to repeat that. Your Honours will know it. It would be stupid to suggest that Keraterm was a holiday camp, and I don't do so for a moment, and I don't want anybody to think that in relation to what we have asserted in the Defence brief or what we say here that it was anything other than a place that was thoroughly unpleasant. Nevertheless, one must remember a number of features. Firstly, in relation to Dusko Sikirica, this particular camp had been established some weeks before he arrived and was placed there to work. Therefore, it can properly be said that the regime which had been established was not one of his creation. Therefore, when he was assigned to Keraterm camp, a culture already existed by the time he got there which was one which would no doubt, Your Honours may feel, be extremely difficult to change once it had been established, particularly if you are given the extent of authority which he was given by Zivko Knezevic. We respectfully submit that because of the extremely limited authority that he was given and because there was already a culture of ill-treatment in place when he arrived there, it was always going to be difficult, if not impossible, for someone of his authority to change that fact. Once the pattern had been established of people such as Zoran Zigic doing what they did, then it was always going to be an uphill task for the most morally courageous individual to change events at Keraterm. We respectfully submit that the actual authority and actual role of Dusko Sikirica was such that there was never a prospect of him being able to do very much about it. Of course, by acts of negligence, in the sense of not doing things, others think that that is the green light for them to act in a similar way, and that is one aspect of why he has had to plead guilty. But we respectfully submit that the authority that he in fact had, and we would submit has to be sentenced upon, was so limited that it was almost non-existent. This leads me to a number of comparisons which we would seek to draw between this case and others. We're conscious, of course, that in a number of judgements, the Tribunal has indicated that it may be invidious to draw comparisons between individual cases, and that is probably so because there are many different cases which come before the Trial Chambers and they depend on essentially different facts. Having said that, we would respectfully remind Your Honours of a number of matters that relate to two cases in particular. The first is the Celebici case, both in its judgement and its appeal. Your Honours will recall or be able to refer back to, in particular, paragraph 717 to 721. Whilst that, no doubt, in the appeal judgement sets out the care with which one has to approach other cases in drawing comparisons, we respectfully submit that if there are comparable facts, then it can be appropriate to make comparisons and to draw similarities between individual cases. And we do submit that both the Celebici case and the Todorovic case are cases which can properly fall into that category. Your Honours, at paragraph 717, the Appeals Chamber in the Celebici appeal indicated that it had a considerable amount of -- the Trial Chamber has a considerable amount of discretion in determining appropriate sentencing. "This is largely," it said, "because of the overriding obligation to individualise the penalty to fit the individual circumstances of the accused and the gravity of the crime. To achieve this goal, Trial Chambers are obliged to consider both aggravating and mitigation circumstances relating to an individual accused. The many circumstances taken into account by Trial Chambers to date are evident if one considers the sentencing judgements which have been rendered. Sentences imposed have been varied." And it then sets out the range of sentences that have been imposed. It goes on in paragraph 719: "It is noted that each party in this case urges the Appeals Chamber to compare their case with others which have already been the subject of final determination in order to persuade the Appeals Chamber to either increase or decrease sentence. Although this will be considered further in the context of individual submissions, the Appeal Chamber notes that, as a general principle, such comparison is often of limited assistance." And this is an important matter: "Whilst it does not disagree with the contention that two accused convicted of similar crimes in similar circumstances should not, in practice, receive very different sentences, often the differences are more significant than the similarities, and the mitigating and aggravating factors dictate different results. They are not reliable as the sole basis for sentencing an individual." So in our respectful submission, there can be, in an appropriate case, a comparison made and comparisons drawn to the assistance of a defendant. Further on in that judgement - and this again is a relevant matter to this submission - at paragraph 756, the Appeals Chamber said this: "Public confidence in the integrity of the administration of criminal justice, whether international or domestic, is a matter of abiding importance to the survival of the institutions which are responsible for that administration. One of the fundamental elements in any rational and fair system of criminal justice is consistency in punishment. This is an important reflection of the notion of equal justice. The experience of many domestic jurisdictions over the years has been that such public confidence may be eroded if these institutions give an appearance of injustice by committing substantial inconsistencies in the punishment of different offenders where the circumstances of the different offences and of the offenders being punished are sufficiently similar that the punishments imposed would, in justice, be expected to be also generally similar. And the following two paragraphs of that judgement are also relevant. We submit that that's a perfectly proper set of principles to apply to the issue of sentence. And it may be appropriate perhaps after lunch - I don't know - to deal with the two cases in which I say there are similarities and upon which the Defence would draw to assist Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can deal with this, Mr. Greaves, which is: If you're going to rely on Todorovic, that was a completely different case. It was not a camp case. And also, significantly, there was powerful mitigation given the time with which the plea was entered and the fact that there was substantial cooperation, factors which are missing in the current case.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'm going to ask Your Honours to let me try and develop an argument against that proposition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, and you will do that in the afternoon. Very well. We'll take the break. We'll resume at 2.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Can I respectfully ask the Chamber how late it will be sitting tonight?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
