utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Greaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, the learned Judge Judge May observed before lunch that there were differences between the Todorovic case and the instant case and cited three matters which I'll deal with, if I may. The first is the issue of when the plea was made. I've already addressed you on that, and I'm not going to go over old ground. As far as the second matter that the learned Judge mentioned, the issue of cooperation, I'm not in a position, and I accept that -- not in a position to advance to you substantial cooperation within the meaning of the -- within the context of the jurisprudence of the Tribunal. The third observation that the learned Judge made was that this was not a camp case, that Todorovic was not a camp case. If I can deal with that. Yes, it wasn't a camp case, but it was a case of persecution, and so a valid comparison can be made with the context into which Keraterm fell within the persecution that took place on a wider scale in Prijedor, and a valid comparison, we submit, can be made between that and the role of Todorovic in the wider persecution that took place and involved a number of other features well above that of simple detention and ill-treatment within a detention facility. The first matter which I would seek to draw a valid comparison between this defendant and the defendant in Todorovic: Todorovic occupied the position of chief of police in Bosanski Samac and was indeed a member of the Crisis Staff. Now, if one was to extrapolate that out into the context of Prijedor, the person who occupied a similar position in Prijedor was the man called Simo Drljaca, a man who was formerly an indictee of this Tribunal, who has subsequently died. He was both the chief of police and a member of the Crisis Staff in Prijedor. So the position which Todorovic occupies and the features which aggravate his participation in persecution are the same as those of Simo Drljaca. This defendant is very much further down the tree compared with Simo Drljaca and is certainly and cannot properly be described as being anything to do with the authorities who are controlling and organising what is taking place. So there is -- it's not a similarity, but it's a proper and valid point of comparison that we draw. The defendant Todorovic exercised a far greater, therefore -- greater and wider authority than this defendant, and one only needs to look at paragraphs 42 to 47 of the judgement that Your Honours gave in that case to see the wider context in which that particular defendant was involved as compared with the one single facility, Keraterm, in which this defendant with what we say is limited authority is dealing. There are other comparisons which one can draw and which are, we submit, relevant and proper to consider. First of all, the defendant in this case did not take part in the sense of being an organiser or leader of the armed takeover of Prijedor. He plainly was a reserve policeman at that time and played his role as a reserve policeman. But I think that at paragraph 35 of the judgement that you gave the Todorovic case, it may be inferred that you were dealing with a rather different participation by that defendant in the armed takeover of power. Secondly, the admission that the defendant Todorovic made concerning murder. I'm not going to go over the facts of that, but the reason why the Defence set out in its sentencing brief the proposition that the murder to which he has admitted was one which was, on the face of it, one which did not -- was not accompanied by prior humiliation and degradation of the victim and nor was there any evidence of the man suffering, was to draw a valid distinction between the nature of the murder in this case and the nature of the murder in Todorovic. The next valid point of comparison that one can make: Although there plainly were, as is agreed in the plea agreement, rapes which took place in Keraterm, there is no suggestion that this defendant took part in them and indeed knew -- or knew of them. That is, of course, a very different position than the case of Mr. Todorovic, who -- and it's set out again - and I don't need to go into the detail of it - at paragraphs 37 and 38, some of the aspects of that. That is absent in this case, so one can draw, we say, a valid comparison with the nature of persecution in this case. And again paragraphs 39, 40, and 41 of that judgement. So if one can draw the strand together, the defendant Todorovic is -- because his superior rank, superior position is involved in a much wider aspect of persecution. And if one was then to take it to the -- and compare it to the case of Prijedor, it would be as if he was responsible for the setting up of Keraterm, Omarska, Trnopolje, the ethnic cleansing which took place in Kozarac, and all the other aspects of the persecution which took place. By using that sort comparison, one can look at the more confined role of the defendant Dusko Sikirica and see where it is that he fits into the -- a similar scheme of things. The other case which -- with which valid comparison, we submit, can be drawn is the Celebici case. That was a camp case, and it involved, as far as the command of the camp was concerned, a man called Pavo Mucic. Now, I'm aware that that's a matter that's pending before this Trial Chamber as well, so I hope that what I say is appropriate, but there were similarities between that case and this. Your Honours just give me a moment, please. If Your Honours recall from the sentencing judgement in -- or the judgement in the Trial Chamber, paragraph 1241: "Celebici prison camp was established to detain those Bosnian Serbs in the Konjic municipality whose loyalty to the State of Bosnia and Herzegovina was in doubt. "The solution to the perceived threat from those arrested during military operations by the Bosnian government forces at, inter alia, Bradina and Donje Selo, was to keep them detained in the Celebici prison camp under the watchful eyes of Bosnian guards who would ensure that they would no longer constitute security risks or any danger to the state. The Trial Chamber has found that the facilities improvised in the Celebici prison camp were not satisfactory, being far from adequate for the number of detainees. Those who were responsible for the detention of the prisoners clearly did not consider the question of suitability of the facility, which was not used as a prison in times of peace. Moreover, the detainees were Bosnian Serbs and those identified as being in opposition to the survival of the independent Bosnian state. Those superintending the prison camp were soldiers of this nascent state, some of whom were zealous for its survival and positively resentful and revengeful for the real or imagined activities --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would you please slow down, Mr. Greaves, when you're reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: "-- real or imagined activities of their opponents. The Trial Chamber found that the conditions of detention in the Celebici prison camp were harsh and indeed inhuman; the feeding conditions were at starvation level; medical health and sanitary conditions were inadequate and indeed deplorable; the guards were hostile, and severe beatings, torture and humiliation of detainees were the norm. Some guards experimented punishment methods on detainees, and the death of detainees was a common occurrence and not a surprise. No one appeared to care whether the detainees survived. These were the conditions perpetrated by Zdravko Mucic, who was the commander of the Celebici prison camp after its creation. "There is evidence that Mr. Mucic selected the guards. He also chose his deputy, Hazim Delic, in apparent demonstration of the type of discipline he expected in the prison camp. In addition, the prison camp was set within the Celebici barracks, where soldiers of the Bosnian army had free access. "The uncontradicted evidence before the Trial Chamber is that Mucic was the commander of the camp, with overall authority over the officers, guards, and detainees, and the person to whom the officers and guards were subordinate. Mr. Mucic was responsible for conditions in the prison camp and for the unlawful confinement of the civilians there detained. He made no effort to prevent or punish those who mistreated the prisoners or even to investigate specific incidents of mistreatment, including the death of detainees. Indeed, there is evidence that he was never in the prison camp at night, when mistreatment was most likely to occur." Your Honours, we submit that, with some obvious distinctions as to elements of personal participation by the defendant Dusko Sikirica, there are considerable similarities between what took place in Celebici and what took place in Keraterm. It's right to say that the numbers of people who were detained in Celebici was rather less. My recollection is that it was in the middle hundreds, around 500 or so, as opposed to the 1.500 or so who were in Keraterm. But, on the other hand, it went on for much longer. It went on from early May until the middle of November, 1992. So that there are proper similarities that can be seen between those two cases, and there is one in particular which may be thought to be one which has a resonance here in this case, and it's this: Mucic was plainly someone who neglected his duties as much as anything, would disappear when things got difficult, would go off either fishing or to see his family, as was observed by the Trial Chamber, and it was through neglect as much as anything, rather than doing positively things to encourage mistreatment to take place, that his responsibility in particular arose. In our submission, there are, as we say, very considerable similarities between those two counts. One difference which might be drawn is that it's implicit in what the Trial Chamber said that Mucic had the power of punishment over the guards who were in that camp; that is to be contrasted with this case, where it is agreed between the parties that the defendant had no power to punish. That's a very important power, of course, because in the absence of a power to punish there and then, it becomes extremely difficult to anybody to exercise proper authority, and in a sense you are sending someone to do a job without giving him the appropriate powers to do it. And that's a point that we make in respect of Sikirica, which is that he wasn't given the tools to do the job properly. He was given 15 men to look after 1.500. And any view of Zivko Knezevic would suggest, we submit, that he was a man who really wasn't interested in giving to Sikirica - or whoever it was at Keraterm - wasn't interested in giving them the appropriate powers to punish, the appropriate powers to administer, the appropriate powers to run the place as it should have been run. It then should come as no surprise that the kind of regime grows up - before the defendant arrives - grows up that leads to the kind of events of which we have heard so much. Your Honour, we draw those comparisons because we respectfully submit that they are valid comparisons and one can look at where do people fit into the various hierarchies, where do they fit into the context of various places? Of course, we don't have the advantage in this case of the defendant cooperating and giving evidence for the Prosecution. I accept that entirely. But if one takes -- to a certain extent balances out the various distinctions between Todorovic and Dusko Sikirica, then some semblance of similarity can begin to appear, we submit, and it is that element and the comparisons that we respectfully draw between that case and Celebici as well which leads us to advocate the sentence of 10 years that we do. Could I now just briefly go into closed session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: There are two short matters. And I've been slightly longer than I've anticipated, which Your Honours can properly take into consideration. The first is you have a report from Mr. McFadden. It's very short, but it's succinct and to the point, indicating that he's been a perfectly good prisoner whilst in detention at the Detention Unit. The second matter is this: He has throughout the trial, I hope, behaved exemplary, in an exemplary fashion, has not shown disrespect in any way to the Tribunal, and although my back is always turned to him, I hope that I can fairly say that he has shown proper respect towards the Tribunal at all times. Your Honours, it's at this point that I would ask for him to be given leave, as you've indicated you will, to speak, and then I'll have just a very brief thing to say and then I will sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Sikirica, you may speak. THE ACCUSED SIKIRICA: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. To begin with, I wish to thank you for giving me this opportunity to address you. I hope you will not mind my reading, because it will be very hard for me to say what I have to say otherwise. Thank you. Before the war in Bosnia, we all lived together in good neighbourly relations regardless of who or what we were. Prijedor was a good place to live in in the former Yugoslavia and to live together. I had many friendships, many of which transcended ethnic differences. When the war broke out, we had to go where we were told to go because we had no choice. We could refuse to obey orders -- do I have to repeat? Unfortunately, when the war broke out, we had to go where we were told to go. We didn't have much choice. We could either obey orders, refuse to obey them, or desert. I was sent to Keraterm, although I would have preferred to go somewhere else at the time, because to go and work in Keraterm was the worst thing that could have happened to me. After the events in 1992, I personally had occasion to see the consequences suffered by Serbian refugees who arrived in Prijedor because of similar events elsewhere, and I was able to imagine what the people who had to leave Prijedor had to go through. I fully understand that these events had destructive consequences and that they still affect Muslims today, some of whom were my friends. After I saw and I understood the consequences, I wish to tell the Trial Chamber that I deeply regret everything that happened in Keraterm while I was there. I feel only regret for all the lives that have been lost and the lives that were damaged in Prijedor, in Keraterm, and unfortunately, I contributed to the destruction of these lives. I am especially sorry that I did not have enough moral courage and power to prevent some or all of the terrible things that happened. I would like to be able to turn back the clock and act differently. I understand that by taking responsibility for my role in these events I have to be punished, and I hope that what happened to me will be a good lesson to anyone anywhere who finds himself in similar circumstances in the future, and I truly hope that I will be forgiven, although I do understand that some will find it very difficult. I also hope that my family will forgive me, because through my thoughtlessness, I have brought their lives into a difficult situation. I hope that what happened to me will contribute to the faster return of Muslims to their homes and to the faster and more efficient reconciliation of all peoples. I understand that as a consequence of this, I will be absent from Prijedor for a long time, but let me assure you, Your Honours, that when I do return home one day, I will be the one to speak with the most conviction against such folly, and I hope that you will accept this -- that you will accept my regret and my remorse for everything that I did and everything I did not do. I feel no self-pity because I know that this is an experience I have to go through, but I trust that Your Honours will understand when I say that I deeply regret what has happened and that I regret that I cannot be with my family in my home. I know that it is always difficult to find enough words and the right words to express one's sorrow in such circumstances, but I hope that Your Honours will understand me and reach a just decision. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit. Mr. Greaves, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, the final matter is simply this: that the Prosecution adverted to what value should be placed on a guilty plea in the absence of remorse. I'm not going to address you as a jury. It's for you to make your minds up what value you place on what the defendant has just said, but I urge you strongly to take it into account. For all the reasons that we've urged, we respectfully submit that an appropriate sentence in this case is one of ten years and that that would justly meet all the circumstances which pertain to this particular defendant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Greaves. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honours, Defence for the accused Damir Dosen has submitted their written sentencing brief dealing in detail with the matters which we believe were important for reaching a decision on the sentence. Now, without repeating what has been covered in our written brief, the Defence now wishes to point out certain relevant aspects. You have in front of you, Your Honours, the accused Damir Dosen born in Prijedor in Bosnia and Herzegovina. He is now aged 34, and at the time of perpetration of the acts, he was 25 years old. He has been now in detention for two years in the UN Detention Unit. He has pleaded guilty Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to count 3 of the second amended indictment. The Defence will now point out the circumstances which it deems relevant to the sentencing decision, all with regard to his guilty plea of the 6th of September this year. Before this Tribunal in various cases, a wide range of views have been expressed on the events that took place in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1992. They are often confronted views, but together they present a fairly clear picture of the events at the time. After almost 50 years of harmonious life in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, almost overnight great changes occurred in this society and in the minds of people. Nationalist oligarchies in all peoples sewed the seeds of internecine and hatred with their unscrupulous propaganda as witnessed by one of the witnesses of the Prosecution. They persuaded people that peaceful coexistence with other peoples was no longer possible, that it was necessary to draw borders and separate themselves from others. They tried to persuade people that the only choice was to fight or to die. Only a few people were able to get away, find shelter, and avoid the horrors of the war. Everyone who remained at home could not isolate themselves from the war turmoil and the political events, and by force of circumstance, many of them were mobilised against their will and pushed into the evil of war which took over this territory. A typical example of this is the period from the beginning of April 1992, when complete chaos and anarchy ruled in the entire territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The same happened throughout that country. Law and order ceased to exist, and human virtue and goodness ceased to exist and gave way to primitivism and deep hatred. This rage left no place for goodness, and the voice of the individual could not be heard because it was deafened by the choir of hatred. This is the place where Damir Dosen found himself, unemployed, a simple soldier without rank, assigned to reserve police forces, and this is the man who is now before you, Your Honours, to bear his share of the burden and punishment for what he has done. Before the beginning of this case, in the indictment and in his opening statement, the Prosecution claimed that Damir Dosen was the leader of the shift in Keraterm, that he personally participated in mistreatment on at least seven occasions, that he encouraged guards on his shift to beat up and torture people, and he willingly allowed them to do it. At that time, the Prosecutor was maintaining that the accused, with his own behaviour, set a very bad example when he omitted to punish the guards under his command for the crimes they perpetrated in the sense of Article 7(1) of the Statute. Regardless of this, independently of this, rather, there were four counts of the indictment against the accused for cruel treatment and torture, and he was acquitted of these counts by a decision of this Trial Chamber. With such counts in the indictment charging him with a key role in mistreatment of non-Serbs and ethnic cleansing of non-Serbian population in the Prijedor municipality, the accused Dosen, at the beginning of this case, had no choice but to start with the proceedings and attempt to prove his innocence of those counts. As it transpired with the plea of the 6th of September, the -- most of the charges contained in the indictment are not contained in the plea agreement, and they're not there because they were not justified. The accused Dosen had the opportunity to establish this only after evidence was adduced at trial to clarify his role in the Keraterm camp, as detailed in section (B) of the plea agreement. As for counts 12 to 15, when evidence was adduced and the Prosecution accepted the realistic role of the accused Damir Dosen in the events, only then did the accused plead guilty to count 3 of the second amended indictment. Today, in an effort to elaborate on some mitigating circumstances, the Defence is going to -- the Prosecution mentions the so-called superior authority that he had in the Keraterm camp and the fact that he did nothing when people were mistreated and beaten up. Today, in his submissions, the Prosecutor especially elaborated on the trust, the public trust, in the accused Dosen as allegedly derived from his position as reserve policeman. The issue of public trust and abuse of that trust are concepts which have been mentioned for the first time today in this courtroom, and neither witnesses for the Prosecution or witnesses for the Defence, or the Prosecution or the Defence counsel, ever mentioned any situation where the accused Dosen, or any other accused in this courtroom, was ever vested with public trust or ever abused it. In the absence of evidence for commanding responsibility or superior authority on the part of Damir Dosen, the Prosecution is trying to paint a different picture of the accused Dosen, although there is no basis for that either in the evidence adduced in front of this Trial Chamber or in the plea agreement. If we speak of the public trust that a certain function entails, then it would be more appropriate to speak of a prominent citizen who was elected to a certain function. It is absolutely inappropriate to speak of the accused Dosen in this way, because the evidence clearly showed that it was purely by legal obligation that Damir Dosen was assigned to the reserve police force. And we should not forget that all this happened during the state of war. This situation could be described only as military duty. In no way could it be an example of public trust. The Defence wishes to underline, and the Prosecution accepts, that he had no special rank, but he did have some authority, they point out, and he did exert it over other guards. The letter of the agreement, however, leaves no doubt as to the role of Damir Dosen in the Keraterm camp. In the agreement, the parties clearly agreed that he had some very limited control over equally ranked guards. The allegations from the agreement and the allegations from the indictment are at great variance. There is no substantial authority that Damir Dosen had. The Prosecution is now trying to introduce a new concept of responsibility which is not based either in the Rules or in the hitherto practice of this Tribunal and as such has to be rejected. There is no word about that in the factual basis. All the allegations by the Office of the Prosecutor cannot be considered as facts established beyond a reasonable doubt. In considering aggravating circumstances, the only allegations that can be taken into account are those accepted in the plea agreement and in the factual basis. It is the opinion of the Trial Chamber in the Celebici case that the only aggravating circumstances that can be taken into account are those proved beyond a reasonable doubt. In this case, those are the facts in the plea agreement. Anything beyond that cannot be taken into account as an aggravating circumstance. The Defence also wishes to stress that there is not a single piece of evidence that Damir Dosen ever personally mistreated, abused, or threatened anyone, or was present when something like that was done, or has ever ordered anything of the kind. The Defence maintains that there are no further aggravating circumstances beyond what is contained in the agreement. What is contained in the agreement is the essence of the act itself and cannot be considered as an aggravating circumstance. That he had command over 6 to 12 people and that he had some limited authority is not an aggravating circumstance. That is the essence of his position there. No other aggravating circumstances were established. Keraterm did exist, but Dosen had no effective role in its control and operation. The conditions in the camp were indeed very difficult, but Dosen was not responsible for providing adequate food, water, medical assistance, or appropriate accommodation. Beatings did occur in the camp, but whenever he could, Dosen tried to prevent them. People who came from outside the camp to mistreat detainees were beyond control. It was not possible to prevent that. The Defence believes that on the part of Damir Dosen, there is a number of mitigating circumstances which must be taken into account, by all means, when meting out the sentence. At the time of the perpetration of the criminal act, Damir Dosen was a young man, only 25 years old. He is the youngest of all the accused standing before this Trial Chamber. At the time, Damir Dosen had only graduated from the primary school. At that age and with such an education, we need not elaborate on his knowledge and personal experience, which must have been modest. At the very outset of the war, he suffered a personal tragedy. He lost a son. That was compounded by the general tragedy which hit Prijedor and Bosnia and Herzegovina. The death of the infant, whom he buried himself, was a hard enough blow, but it was not the only one. He was assigned to be a guard, a security guard, at the facility where his neighbours and friends were detained only because they were non-Serbs. He was not brought up to discriminate people because of their ethnic background or religion. His whole life he socialised with everyone, regardless of their ethnic background, and all the witnesses, both for the Prosecution and the Defence, testified that this was a situation which was new and difficult for him. He could not avoid the military call-up. He had nowhere to hide and he had no means of avoiding the mobilisation. At home he had a wife who was shattered by pain. At work, he was surrounded by people who had to choose between mobilisation and prison. Torn by his personal tragedy and problems at work, he was at a loss. When he was assigned at Keraterm, he was told that it would last only for a few days and that people who were taken there to give a statement would soon be released. Dosen, as a reserve policeman, did not know what was happening around him. He couldn't understand. Nor did he know how long it would last. As we heard from both Prosecution and Defence witnesses, he believed, as they were told too, that they would just be interviewed and then let go home. He saw, instead, people who were beaten, hungry, ignorant of the fate of their loved ones. In the conditions that prevailed, he did the only thing possible: He tried to make things easier for them, to encourage them, to make it possible for them to call home, to receive packages with food, sometimes to go out of the premises and to use as much water as was available. He also tried to protect them from mistreatment, as much as he could and whenever he could, and that too was confirmed by numerous witnesses for both the Prosecution and the Defence. When Dosen was on duty, people were unafraid to go out and to receive packages with food and clothing brought by the families. People could, without fear, communicate with him, approach him, and ask him for help. He was always kind and friendly when talking to them. Dosen helped them get medical help, and that too was confirmed by a number of witnesses for both the Prosecution and the Defence. Dosen did all of this regardless of whether he had known those people from before or not. That was the way he acted towards everyone: towards people from Prijedor, Kozarac, Ljubija, Gomjenica, Cerik, or Puharska. There are more than enough people who testified to this before this Trial Chamber, and the Defence covered it in detail in its written submission. You have already had opportunity to hear from over 20 people who had been detained there and who, each from their own perspective, described a man who helped them, protected them, and defended them. The Trial Chamber will certainly remember the tears in the eyes of witnesses who spoke about Dosen: Witness A, Witness DP, and Witness Husein Ganic. In all three cases, those were elderly people with great life experience who could not contain the tears and the emotion. The Trial Chamber will remember that all of seven witnesses, former detainees, testified in favour of Damir Dosen, despite the fear of how their testimony would be taken by their compatriots, despite the fact that some of them travelled from Sweden and other foreign countries, travelling for two or three days, although they had not known Damir Dosen from before the war. You will certainly remember Husein Ganic, who testified as a witness for the Prosecution in the Omarska case and who testified in this case about how Dosen saved his and his son's life. The Trial Chamber will certainly remember Petar Sovilj as well, who testified as to how Dosen saved the Crnalic family, who he had not known before the attack on Prijedor. All of this just goes to prove the claim of the Defence that all of Dosen's life before the war goes to prove -- is a mitigating circumstance. None of this is a coincidence, because even at the time when he worked in Keraterm, on numerous occasions Dosen expressed remorse and regret over what was happening. People recognised the truth and honesty of his words. Dosen felt remorse while Keraterm was still in existence, while nobody else was doing so, when this was something exceptional, something risky and dangerous. His remorse is deep and sincere. It was deep and sincere then and it is still so today, and we feel that his sincerity is a mitigating circumstance. The Prosecutor today mentioned a witness who said, "Yes, they deserved it," meaning the inmates of Room 3, but the Prosecutor did not quote the entire testimony in which Dosen said that he regretted what had happened and offered to help. All the other Prosecution witnesses who testified to this, quoted by the Defence in our submission, spoke of this very convincingly. They were people from various rooms to whom Dosen expressed his regret in the same terms, and none of them ever mentioned anything like what the Prosecutor mentioned today. Your Honours, please remember Witness A, who wept in this courtroom, touched by the sincere actions of Dosen in that difficult situation. The witness mentioned by the Prosecutor today simply could not believe that someone felt regret at the time and apologised even then, thus publicly distancing himself from others. The Prosecutor also mentions the psychiatric report, which erroneously represents Dosen's attitude towards his guilt which he has expressed clearly here. The Defence begs the Chamber to take as a mitigating circumstance the character of Damir Dosen. Numerous witnesses, both for the Prosecution and Defence, spoke of Dosen as a young man who behaved well, who was -- who had good manners, who came from a good family, and who kept company with everyone regardless of ethnic background. He was interested in motorcycles and in pigeon-keeping. He was a good and a decent man both before, during, and Keraterm. Damir Dosen is a family man. He has a wife and two young children, two sons: Mitar, aged 8 and David, aged 16 months. Mitar was born under difficult wartime circumstances, and Damir a few months after his arrest. The present situation in the family is only a continuation of the difficult circumstances that have prevailed in his life since 1992. During the war, Zoran Zigic killed for no reason at all Dosen's sister. Three months after his arrest, Dosen's father died of a sudden heart attack. Today, Dosen's family consists of his unemployed wife, his two sons, and his mother, who is mentally ill, and they live in Prijedor in very difficult material circumstances. The Defence considers his family circumstances to be a significant mitigating factor. The reports of psychiatrists and psychologists, who are expert witnesses here, show that the mental state of Dosen, both before, during, and after the commission of the crimes represent a number of stresses and traumas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, you mentioned that during the war, Zoran Zigic killed the sister of the accused. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Zoran Zigic, and I think we heard testimony about this, I cannot now remember, but I think it was a Defence witness whose name I could mention in closed session, but this was testimony that was heard here and it's a fact. It was not actually his sister, but his cousin. His cousin in the first -- his first cousin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can you find it in the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Before the end of my closing statement, I will learn the name. I will ask my colleague to find where in the testimony, in the transcript we heard this fact. May we now go into closed session so I can tell you the name of the witness in question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The psychiatrist and psychologist who are expert witnesses found that the mental state of the accused represents a whole series of multiple stresses and traumas both before, during, and after the commission, and this situation seriously compromised the ability of the accused to react appropriately to the circumstances in which he found himself. Soon afterwards, the accused started suffering from post-traumatic stress syndrome. The mental status of the accused, both during the commission of the acts and today, is a major mitigating circumstance. The Defence feels it has proved the continuity of psychological problems from the death of his first child until today, and we have written proofs which we have adduced to show this. Dosen has been in the UN detention centre for two years, and throughout this time, there have been no complaints about his behaviour and his bearing in the Detention Unit, which is a further mitigating circumstance. The accused Dosen pleaded guilty when he was in a situation to do so in relation to acts he had actually committed, and we have already spoken of the reasons for this. By pleading guilty, he has shown that he's sincere and honest. He's fully aware of far-reaching consequences of his plea, the consequences of his actions. In a situation in which the wounds of war are still open and are still painful, only a person who can understand the sufferings of others is able to stand up and admit his guilt to the world. This personal act by this young and courageous man is an example to all those who should stand up and confess their guilt, thus contributing to what is so sorely needed in Bosnia and Herzegovina today: truth, justice, and reconciliation. With this act, Dosen has greatly contributed to the fact that in Prijedor today, people are speaking much more freely about crime and responsibility for crimes. And in this way, he's contributing to the goals of this International Tribunal, and those are truth and reconciliation. With his guilty plea and his agreement with the Prosecution, he has helped to shorten these proceedings, and in addition, he has waived his right to an appeal in the event that the Trial Chamber decides to pronounce a sentence within the limits set by the plea agreement. I would now like to ask to go into private session for a moment.

utterances.text: Yes. Private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are we still in closed session, Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's go back to closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I wish to ask the Trial Chamber to allow Damir Dosen to address the Chamber with a few words before I conclude my closing statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, he may.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Dosen. You may speak. THE ACCUSED DOSEN: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Your Honours, at the end of this trial, for the evil that happened in my town Prijedor and in Keraterm, I wish to thank you for letting my voice be remembered. I wish to say that I was in Keraterm, that I was sent there as a reserve policeman, that I spent two months there guarding innocent people who were imprisoned there. I wish to say that at that time I was young, thoughtless, that I had lost a son, that I was caught in the chaos of war and death in which I found it difficult to find my bearings. The people who are imprisoned were my fellow townspeople. They were innocent and they were suffering grievously. A crime has been committed against these people, and I am prepared to take my part of the responsibility for this crime before God and before men. I tried to help them, to make it easier for them, to talk to them, to protect them. The conditions under which they were imprisoned were below human dignity. I am guilty because I agreed to be in Keraterm. I am guilty because I did not help them more. For this I am guilty before God, before those people, and before you, Your Honours. I am sorry for every man who suffered, every family that lost a family member, every child that has lost a father. I am sorry for every mother who has lost a son. I want everybody to hear my words, especially my neighbours, who are imprisoned only because they were not Serbs. Evil happened, and evil must not happen again, nor must it be forgotten. I am conscious of all this today. I'm conscious that a man, however small and impotent he may be, must not allow himself to be overcome by lack of courage and that he must sacrifice himself in such situations. This is the only way in which we can help future generations to overcome injustice and inhuman actions. I wish to thank Their Honours and the gentlemen from the Prosecution for their efforts to reach the truth and to satisfy justice. I hope that the Trial Chamber will give me a chance to return to my family and to my children, to return to my neighbours of all religious and nationalities, and I hope that we will again have an opportunity to live in my town of Prijedor with my fellow townspeople with whom I lived and kept company before the war. I hope that we shall live together again in harmony, as we did before the war and before the evil that befell us. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence would also like to thank the esteemed Trial Chamber for their dedication and commitment to establish the truth and satisfy justice in this difficult Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. case. The Defence is also convinced that the accused Dosen has demonstrated his full respect and appreciation of this Court. Once he is released from prison, the Defence firmly believes that he will be a good citizen and contribute to the reconciliation of peoples, and we strongly recommend a sentence of five years.
